South Holland's population increased by around 6,900 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 95,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of South Holland increased by 7.8%, from around 88,300 in 2011 to around 95,100 in 2021.

The population here increased at a similar rate to the overall population of the East Midlands (7.7%), but by a greater percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, South Holland was home to around 0.9 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 0.8 in 2011. This area was among the lowest 10% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was similar in South Holland to the East Midlands as a whole

Median age in South Holland

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of South Holland increased by one year, from 45 to 46 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the East Midlands as a whole in 2021 (41 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by around 2,300 (an increase of 12.8%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 1,100 (6.3% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 1.0 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Employment in South Holland

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed increased in South Holland, but fell across the East Midlands.

In South Holland, the percentage who were employed rose from 55.7% in 2011 to 56.3% in 2021. During the same period, the regional percentage fell from 56.1% to 55.1%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in South Holland fell from 3.5% to 2.2%, while the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were retired (economically inactive) decreased from 28.3% to 27.4%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in South Holland increased by 0.6 percentage points

South Holland stood out from other areas for working hours

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week fell here, but rose across England.

In South Holland, the percentage that worked 15 hours or less in a week fell from 8.8% in 2011 to 8.4% in 2021, while across England it rose from 9.7% to 10.3%. During the same period, the regional percentage remained at 9.8%.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in South Holland fell from 17.8% to 15.1%, while the percentage of adults in employment who worked 31 to 48 hours increased from 55.7% to 58.9%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in South Holland decreased by 0.4 percentage points

South Holland residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 79,600 South Holland residents said they were born in England. This represented 83.7% of the local population. The figure has risen from around 78,000 in 2011, which at the time represented 88.4% of South Holland's population.

Poland was the next most represented, with around 3,800 South Holland residents reporting this country of birth (4.0%). This figure was up from just under 2,800 in 2011, which at the time represented 3.2% of the population of South Holland.

The number of South Holland residents born in Lithuania rose from just over 1,200 in 2011 (1.4% of the local population) to around 2,500 in 2021 (2.6%).

In 2021, 83.7% of South Holland residents reported their country of birth as England

Fewer couples without children

South Holland saw the East Midlands' joint third-largest percentage-point fall (alongside Oadby and Wigston and West Lindsey) in the proportion of households including a couple but no children (from 22.4% in 2011 to 20.2% in 2021).

Across the region, only Rutland (from 22.3% to 19.8%) and South Kesteven (from 22.2% to 19.8%) saw a greater decrease in the percentage of households including a couple but no children.

Despite the decrease, South Holland was in the highest 10% of English local authority areas for the share of households including a couple but no children in 2021.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in South Holland decreased by 2.2 percentage points

Changing relationships in South Holland

South Holland saw the East Midlands' joint third-largest percentage-point rise (alongside Hinckley and Bosworth, Melton and West Lindsey) in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership (from 9.7% in 2011 to 10.6% in 2021).

Across the region, only North East Derbyshire (from 9.2% to 10.3%) and South Kesteven (from 9.9% to 10.8%) saw a greater increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership in South Holland increased by 0.8 percentage points

National identity in South Holland

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater in nearby Boston (6.9 percentage points) than in South Holland (3.7 percentage points).

In South Holland, the percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity increased from 7.9% in 2011 to 11.6% in 2021. During the same period, the percentage in nearby Boston increased from 14.0% to 20.9%.

The percentage of people who identified with a UK and non-UK national identity in South Holland increased from 0.3% to 1.2%, while the percentage of people who identified as "British only" increased from 11.2% to 46.6%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in South Holland increased by 3.7 percentage points

Rise in private renting

Of South Holland households, 17.1% rented privately in 2021, up from 12.7% in 2011.

The increase in the percentage of privately-rented homes was greater in South Holland (4.4 percentage points) than across the East Midlands (3.8 percentage points, from 14.9% to 18.7%). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.6 percentage points, from 16.8% to 20.5%.

Private renting in South Holland increased by 4.4 percentage points

Unpaid care in South Holland

In 2021, 4.2% of South Holland residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 6.6% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 50 people (1.9%) reported providing between 20 and 49 hours of unpaid care each week, compared with 1.5% in 2011. The proportion of South Holland residents (aged five years and over) that provided at least 50 hours of weekly unpaid care increased from 2.8% to 3.1%.

The decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care was greater across the East Midlands (2.8 percentage points, from 7.4% to 4.6%) than in South Holland (2.4 percentage points). Across England, the proportion fell by 2.8 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in South Holland decreased by 2.4 percentage points

Religion in South Holland

In 2021, 33.0% of South Holland residents reported having "No religion", up from 19.4% in 2011. The rise of 13.6 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in South Holland. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the East Midlands, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.5% to 40.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 58.9% of people in South Holland described themselves as Christian (down from 72.3%), while 6.5% did not state their religion (down from 7.2% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 33.0% of usual residents in South Holland reported having "No religion"

Health in South Holland

In 2021, 43.4% of South Holland residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 42.1% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 37.6% to 37.5%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of South Holland residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.1% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 4.4% to 4.1%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very bad health in South Holland decreased by 0.2 percentage points

Disability in South Holland

In 2021, 7.2% of South Holland residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 8.7% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just over 1 in 10 people (10.4%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 10.3% in 2011. The proportion of South Holland residents who were not disabled increased from 81.1% to 82.4%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in South Holland (1.5 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the East Midlands (1.6 percentage points, from 9.3% to 7.7%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in South Holland decreased by 1.5 percentage points

Ethnic groups in South Holland

In 2021, 0.6% of South Holland residents identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group"), up from 0.1% in 2011. The 0.5 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the East Midlands, the percentage of people from the "Other ethnic groups" ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.6% to 1.3%, while across England the percentage increased from 1.0% to 2.2%.

In 2021, 96.3% of people in South Holland identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 97.8% in 2011), while 1.3% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 0.9% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category increased from 0.8% in 2011 to 1.2% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
